newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya government bans "illegal" mass rally.
newsitem.headline: Kenya government bans "illegal" mass rally.

text.p: Kenya's government declared illegal on Friday a mass rally called by a coalition of opposition and church groups demanding constitutional change.
The government warned the public not to attend the rally, set for Saturday, and said anyone attending would "face the full force of the law".
But Kenneth Matiba, a leading opposition leader and proponent of constitutional change, said the opposition would go ahead with the rally.
"The rally is going ahead on Saturday whether (President Daniel arap) Moi likes it or not," Matiba told Reuters through his spokesman.
"The issue of the constitution is very serious and cannot be decided by one man or his party alone. Moi will be responsible for what will happen on Saturday," Matiba added.
Matiba is the chairman of the opposition FORD-Asili party and is one the East African nation's leading businessmen.
The ban and Matiba's remarks threatens a confrontation between protesters and security forces who beat opposition politicians and demonstrators earlier this month to stop a similar rally.

The National Convention Assembly (NCA), an umbrella for Protestant and Catholic church leaders and opposition parties, called the rally to press for a minimum package of constitutional reform before elections later this year.

"The government would like to inform members of the public that the convenors of the intended Uhuru Park (Nairobi) meeting have neither sought nor been given any licence to hold the meeting," said a government statement.
"It is therefore illegal for any person to attend such a meeting," it said, warning diplomats not to meddle in Kenya's internal affairs by attending.
The meeting's organisers intend to provoke a confrontation with the security forces to discredit the government and criminals would take advantage of the rally to loot, the statement said.
"During the ensuing fracas, the organisers would be delighted to see some attendants wounded, arrested or killed only to turn around and blame it on the government," it said.
The NCA decided in April to hold unlicensed public meetings to circumvent a Public Order Act which diplomats, human rights groups and opposition politicians say is deployed to suppress dissent.

"We have not applied for a licence because it is not necessary. Our meeting will be an educational meeting," Kibutha Kibwana, chairman of the NCA's National Convention Executive Council, told a news conference this week.
Kibwana called on a shadowy group known as "Jeshi la Mzee" (Moi's army) not to disrupt the meeting.

President Moi must call presidential and parliamentary elections by the end of the year, pitting the ruling Kenya African National Union (Kanu) against an opposition divided along ethnic, political and personal lines.
Church leaders called for reform last Sunday, despite condemnation from Moi who said the churches' call amounted to an ultimatum and was dictatorial.
